top_choice_rationale: Michon is first on voice and form. His compressed, intensely worked French sentence and one coherent project (vocation, obscure lives, the traces of the dead) run from Vies minuscules and Les Onze through the later books. Round 2 showed that those later books vary the formal solution, moving between the biographical fragment, the rural novel and the court or revolutionary tableau. I read that as development under one method, not repetition, which supports sustained quality. Significance across the whole body of work is the harder criterion. I rest it on the sentences and structure, not on corpus size or colleague support, and I keep the citation narrow. Cărtărescu is a close second. Palm's and Swärd's account of Blinding and Solenoid as different structures answers my repetition worry, and his longer record is the strongest argument against my own pick. Wright is third because her formal departure from Indigenous oral practice is serious, but a few very large novels give a thinner base for a whole-oeuvre citation. I cannot judge Adonis's Arabic prosody directly, so I place him fourth; a specialist report on the originals could change that. No award is last because several candidates meet the standard. All judgments rest on public knowledge and translation. I have not independently verified any text, and the later works of Michon, Cărtărescu and Wright remain unassessed.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; my Prague and Vienna ties, my Dagens Nyheter criticism and my election alongside Carlberg link me to no shortlisted writer, and my own documentary historical fiction is context only, not evidence of preference
